鈴川"The Rokuhara Shogunate is a popular name, taken from its original location in Rokuhara, Kyoto. Officially, it is the Rikuefu... However."
鈴川"Here we come to an odd point. Originally, no office called the Six Guard Offices existed."
鈴川"Six Guard Offices meant the Left and Right Imperial Guards, the Left and Right Military Guards, and the Left and Right Gate Guards. Six capital-defense forces, collectively. Not one organization called the Six Guard Offices. Six, not one: an important distinction."
鈴川"But a Supreme Commander of the Six Guards was appointed to command the six. Later, the post also assumed leadership of the warriors. Under that commander, a staff organization centered on warriors came into being."
鈴川"That organization, people came to call the Six Guard Offices. One organization with the collective name of six others... That is how the name settled."

鈴川"Like the shogun, the Supreme Commander of the Six Guards has authority to impose military government."
鈴川"But not over the same territory. The shogun's authority concerns occupied land acquired on campaign. The Supreme Commander's concerns regions judged necessary during a defensive war against an outside enemy."
鈴川"Both are temporary powers. Wartime only. When war ends, administrative authority returns to the Court. Temporary means that, not merely a pleasing word in the title."
鈴川"The Kamakura Shogunate, however, interpreted the shogun's power broadly. Broadly enough to extend its administration over the whole country and make it permanent."
鈴川"Rokuhara did the same. 'A time of national crisis': under that justification, temporary emergency powers expanded into a claim to indefinite administration over all Yamato. Temporary authority, indefinite duration. The distinction has become rather convenient."

Any student regularly entering this room must be either exceptionally good or exceptionally troublesome.

I was neither. An uninteresting, standard-issue student. Naturally this was my first visit to the principal's office. No particular emotion arose, though.

Just a dry, uninteresting room.

Nothing entertaining about its owner, either. As for what he had to say, that was the exact opposite of entertainment.

To some extent, I had guessed it on the way.

Rules broken, clearly. We were students; no amount of explaining would change that fact.

...So attack from here, make the whole account one-sided. That was the plan, was it?

Scold us, fine. A punishment that stopped us moving about, not fine at all. Home confinement, families informed—then how would we keep searching for Ritsu?

Some clever defense, please. None within reach. Tadayasu, reliable at such times supposedly, was also keeping quiet. Probably he had seen which way this was going. No use putting a hand into it, he must have thought.

What kind of thing was this!

Your argument makes sense. Haan, agreed. No gap left for answering, agreed!

Me. Here. Now!

Say that much, and the answer would be: can't explain? Your fault. Naturally, the ones who can would say so.

Meaning, in the end, whoever has the working tongue wins, no?

Or whoever can knock down the fellow objecting.

Neither skill you possess? Then chup, obey. Is that the arrangement?

A right society? This was a right society!?

Yes, I know. I know, I know, I KNOW.

Not right, but comparatively right!

Better than a society that gets caught up in fellows like me and can't move forward or back. I understand that much!

Understanding, though—accepting was another matter!

Abhi? Now, at this very moment—how could I accept it!?

The principal had to nod.

Exactly what he had been saying until a moment ago.

But nod, he couldn't. Not facing Suzukawa now.

...To be frank, I thought there was something unfair about Suzukawa's tactics.

Using your own misfortune as a shield to push a demand—if the other person caused it, that was different. Otherwise, you could hardly escape the accusation of a low trick. Taking advantage of someone's conscience.

The violence of the weak.

But Suzukawa did not ordinarily do that. Never once had I heard about his past from his own mouth. The vow, I had learned of only today.

Perhaps he had told nobody.

Why speak now? Surely not a sudden wish to buy sympathy.

To help us.
